stories.title: DeepMind agents cut quantum algorithm costs, with Lean-checked proofs
stories.plain: Google DeepMind says teams of Gemini 4 agents found cheaper ways to run several quantum algorithms, from basic arithmetic to chemistry and fusion simulations. Every improved circuit comes with a machine-checked proof that it still computes the right thing, and the proof library is open source.
stories.eng: Agents search over quantum circuit implementations and must emit a Lean proof that each rewritten program matches its specification before a result counts, so the search cannot 'win' with a subtly wrong circuit. Gains are measured as resource estimates (gate cost and qubit count) for fault-tolerant hardware, not runs on a real machine. This builds on a Google preprint from early November; the new release adds chemistry results and the open Lean library on GitHub.
stories.point: The point: AI search plus formal proofs is shrinking the hardware a useful quantum computer needs, which moves the date quantum becomes practical.
stories.means: Quantum algorithms are usually judged by how many qubits and expensive gates they need on an error-corrected machine; today's estimates for useful chemistry are far beyond current hardware. Cutting those costs by an order of magnitude is roughly equivalent to several years of hardware progress. The catch with letting AI optimise circuits is that a faster circuit that is slightly wrong is worthless, and quantum programs are hard to test. Requiring a Lean proof for every result removes that doubt. These are paper estimates for future machines, not demonstrations on real qubits.
stories.industry: Labs are racing to show AI can do original scientific work, and quantum resource estimation is a clean target because results are checkable. It also feeds investor timelines for quantum companies: fewer qubits needed means earlier commercial use cases, especially in chemistry and drug discovery.
stories.you: The pattern to copy is 'search freely, accept only what a checker proves'. If you build agents that optimise code, pair them with a verifier they cannot bypass (formal proofs, property tests, differential tests) rather than trusting benchmark speedups.
terms: Lean
A programming language and proof assistant where a computer checks every step of a mathematical proof.
Resource estimate
A calculation of how many qubits and gates an algorithm would need on a future error-corrected quantum computer.
stories.why: The Lean-verified approach first appeared in a 6 Nov Google preprint reporting up to 290x and 11x gains.
stories.source: The Next Web (via AI Weekly) · 23 Nov; AI Agent Store · 24 Nov

stories.title: OpenAI proposes perplexity as a shared yardstick and a pause line
stories.plain: OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki published internal measurements of how well successive OpenAI models predict text, and proposed the whole industry track this number. He suggests labs agree not to push models past a set level until safety monitoring catches up.
stories.eng: The metric is next-token perplexity on held-out data: how surprised the model is by the next token, with lower meaning better prediction. OpenAI's reported scores fall from about 0.99 for GPT-3.5 and 0.91 for GPT-4 to below 0.8 for recent models, and about 0.76 for the models behind recent open-math results. The proposal is a 0.68–0.70 window that labs would not cross, and a warning that 2027 could bring an 'avalanche' of pretraining advances.
stories.point: The point: OpenAI is offering one simple, measurable capability number that labs could agree to cap, instead of arguing over benchmarks.
stories.means: Benchmarks saturate and can be gamed, so it is hard to say how capable a model is or to write a rule around it. Perplexity is old and dull, but it is measured during training for every model and tracks raw predictive ability well. OpenAI is saying the number has kept falling steadily and that the jumps in capability (like recent maths results) line up with it. The exact scale of these scores depends on OpenAI's evaluation data and normalisation, so they are only comparable within OpenAI's own measurements unless others adopt the same setup.
stories.industry: This lands in a week where METR warned that testing is falling behind capability, and while governments debate compute-based thresholds. A training-time metric is something regulators and labs could audit, but it would require competitors to share data they treat as secret, and open-model advocates are likely to see it as a lever against them.
stories.you: Expect 'what perplexity did this model reach' to start appearing in model cards and policy debates. For your own work, perplexity on your domain's text is still a cheap, useful sanity check when comparing or fine-tuning models.
terms: Perplexity
A measure of how well a language model predicts the next token; lower means better prediction.
Held-out data
Text the model never saw in training, used so the score reflects generalisation, not memory.
stories.why: Yann LeCun separately accused Anthropic's CEO of hyping AI danger to restrict open models, the top Hacker News story on 23 Nov.
stories.source: OpenAI (via AI Weekly, The Neuron) · 23 Nov

stories.title: Nari Labs squeezes a 27B coding model into 10 GB at 3 bits
stories.plain: Nari Labs released a compressed version of the open Qwen3.8-27B model that is about a fifth of the original size. It reports scores on coding and maths tests that match or slightly beat the full-size model.
stories.eng: NariQ stores weights at about 3 bits each in GGUF format, shrinking the model from 53.8 GB in BF16 to 10.12 GB, small enough for a single consumer GPU or a laptop with unified memory. It runs only on Nari's custom fork of llama.cpp, not mainline. Reported scores: DeepSWE v1.1 41.0% vs 39.8%, Terminal-Bench 2.1 63.8 vs 62.6, AIME 25+26 98.3 vs 97.7.
stories.point: The point: a capable open coding model now fits comfortably on hardware many engineers already own.
stories.means: Model weights are normally stored at 16 bits; quantisation rounds them to fewer bits so the model needs less memory and runs faster, usually at some cost in quality. Below 4 bits that cost has typically been noticeable. Nari claims no loss, even a small gain, which is within normal benchmark noise. These are the publisher's own numbers on a model card with no paper, and the slight 'improvement' should be read as 'about equal', not better.
stories.industry: Local inference is gaining ground as API prices, rate limits and data-leak worries (like this week's OpenRouter provider incidents) push teams to run models themselves. Better low-bit quantisation directly lowers the hardware bar for that.
stories.you: If you have a 12–16 GB GPU or a 32 GB Mac, this is worth trying as a private coding assistant. Run it against your own tasks before trusting the benchmark parity, and note the fork dependency before building on it.
terms: Quantisation
Storing model weights with fewer bits to cut memory use and speed up inference.
GGUF
A file format for quantised models used by llama.cpp and tools built on it.
stories.why: A separate Kingy AI test this week found an RTX 5090 runs Qwen3.8-27B at 105.3 tokens per second in llama.cpp.
stories.source: Hugging Face model card (via AI Weekly) · 23 Nov

stories.title: Google checks every agent tool call against plain-English policies
stories.plain: Google's agent platform can now judge each action an agent is about to take against business rules written in ordinary language, and block it before it runs. Google's case study says this cut successful attacks on a standard test from about half to under 1%.
stories.eng: Semantic Governance Policies sit in Agent Gateway, which intercepts traffic between user, agent, model and tools. Policies are YAML files with target_tools, natural-language constraints and an enforcement action such as BLOCK; an LLM evaluates each proposed call against the policy, user intent and conversation history, and a DENY suppresses the call before credentials or APIs are touched. It works alongside Model Armor (prompt and response screening) and Agent Anomaly Detection (session-level telemetry analysis).
specs: in-agent tools, APIs and MCP servers
stories.point: The point: agent security is moving from filtering text to checking the meaning of each action before it happens.
stories.means: Prompt injection works because a model cannot reliably tell instructions from data, so hidden text in an email or web page can steer an agent. Regex filters and allowlists catch known patterns but miss polite social engineering, like asking for a refund the rules forbid, or attacks spread over many turns. Google's approach accepts that the agent may be fooled and adds a separate judge that asks 'does this action fit the rules and what the user wanted?'. AgentDojo is a standard benchmark of injection attacks on tool-using agents; dropping from 48.7% to 0.9% is large, but these are Google's own figures.
stories.industry: Every big platform is now building a control layer between agents and the systems they touch, because banks and enterprises are making customers liable for agent actions. A policy judge that business staff can edit without redeploying is a direct answer to that demand.
stories.you: Separate 'what the agent decides' from 'what is allowed to execute'. Even without Google's platform, you can put a second, cheaper model or rule engine in front of risky tools (payments, deletes, external sends) and log every verdict.
terms: Prompt injection
Hidden instructions in content an AI reads that hijack what it does.
AgentDojo
A benchmark that measures how often attacks make tool-using agents take harmful actions.
Agent Gateway
Google's enforcement point that intercepts and governs an agent's model and tool traffic.
stories.why: Google's developer blog walks through a refund agent where the policy blocks a $120 licence refund that passes every deterministic check.
stories.source: Google technical case study (via AI Agent Store) · 24 Nov; Google Developers Blog

stories.title: AWS swaps Claude for small open 'decider' models inside agents
stories.plain: AWS released five small open-weight models built only to make the routine yes/no and routing decisions inside AI agents. AWS says using them internally instead of Claude Sonnet 4.6 cut labelling costs by 98%.
stories.eng: Strands Decider v2 is a family of five models fine-tuned from Google's open Gemma 4, up to 31B parameters, trained on 17.5 million examples, released under Apache 2.0. They handle classification, routing and approval steps so a frontier model is only called for open-ended work. AWS also extended its Strands Box sandbox, via a Box CLI, to Claude Code, OpenAI Codex and Kiro CLI.
stories.point: The point: production agents are being split into a big model for thinking and small, cheap models for the many routine decisions.
stories.means: A typical agent makes dozens of small calls per task: is this ticket urgent, which tool fits, is this output acceptable. Sending each to a frontier model is slow and expensive. Fine-tuning a smaller model on millions of examples of those exact decisions can match quality for that narrow job at a fraction of the cost. The 98% and 78% figures are AWS's own internal results, not an independent test.
stories.industry: Inference cost is now the main constraint on agent deployments, and every cloud is pushing ways to route around expensive frontier calls. It is also notable that AWS, Anthropic's biggest partner, built this on Google's open model and benchmarked against Claude.
stories.you: Profile your agent's calls: if most are classifications or routing, a small fine-tuned or open model can take them. Keep the frontier model for planning and writing, and measure decision accuracy on your own data before switching.
terms: Open-weight model
A model whose trained parameters are published so anyone can run or fine-tune it.
Routing
Deciding which tool, model or handler should deal with a request.
stories.why: AWS CEO Matt Garman also argued this week that containment, logging and per-agent identities should be deployed now.

stories.title: X Square's WALL-OSS 1.0 robot model handles 55% of new tasks cold
stories.plain: Robotics startup X Square Robot introduced WALL-OSS 1.0, a model that turns camera images and spoken instructions into robot movements. It succeeded on 55.1% of 312 real-robot tasks it had not been trained on.
stories.eng: WALL-OSS 1.0 is a vision-language-action model built on Alibaba's Qwen3.5: it reads images and text and outputs motor actions. Besides the main model there are Lite (4B) and Nano (2B) variants for on-robot use. It scored 67.55/100 on the X2Real benchmark; code and weights are promised 'soon', not yet released.
stories.point: The point: open robot foundation models are getting good enough to do half of unseen real-world tasks without task-specific training.
stories.means: Robots have traditionally been programmed or trained for one job at a time. Vision-language-action models try to do for robots what LLMs did for text: one general model that follows instructions on new tasks. 'Zero-shot' means it had no examples of those specific tasks. 55% is far from reliable enough for a factory, but it is a useful starting point for fine-tuning. Results are company-reported, and until weights ship they cannot be checked.
stories.industry: Robot brains are the current hot spot in physical AI, with Runway's Praxis-1, Nvidia's Isaac stack and many startups competing. Models built on open bases like Qwen are making open weights a large part of that race.
stories.you: If you work near robotics, small 2–4B action models are the ones to watch, since they can run on the robot itself. Wait for the released weights and independent results before planning around it.
terms: Vision-language-action model (VLA)
A model that takes images and instructions as input and outputs robot actions.
Zero-shot
Doing a task with no training examples of that specific task.
stories.why: South Korea opened its first humanoid 'data factory' the same day, with 12 teleoperated bipedal robots collecting training data.

stories.title: Nvidia's board reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO
stories.plain: Nvidia's board voted unanimously to bring Jensen Huang back as president, CEO and director, saying it found no national security risk. He will testify publicly before the Senate on 3 December about export controls.
stories.eng: The board cited input from senior levels of the US government; President Trump joined the board meeting by phone and later said Huang 'did nothing wrong'. Interim CEO Colette Kress returns to her CFO role. A foreign-intelligence probe and a Wachtell-led internal investigation continue, and the board has opened a search for a Chief Compliance Officer.
specs: foreign-intelligence probe; Wachtell review; compliance officer search
stories.point: The point: the most important company in AI hardware has its founder back, but the investigations around him are not over.
stories.means: Nvidia supplies most of the chips used to train and run large AI models, so its leadership and its standing with Washington matter to the whole industry. Huang stepped aside during a foreign-intelligence probe, and the Senate hearing he faces is about export controls on AI chips, the same issue behind this week's Commerce move to blacklist Singapore-based Megaspeed over chip smuggling. The reinstatement removes immediate leadership uncertainty. The White House's direct involvement and the still-open probes mean the story is political as much as corporate.
stories.industry: AI stocks slid into a correction last week amid reports of an SEC look at Nvidia's accounting. Chip supply, export rules and Nvidia's relationship with the US government directly affect how much compute labs can buy and where.
stories.you: Little changes day to day, but export-control rules decide which GPUs are sold where and at what price. If your team buys or rents GPUs abroad, watch the 2–3 December hearings for signs of tighter licensing.
terms: Export controls
Government rules limiting which countries can buy certain technologies, such as advanced AI chips.
Entity list
A US blacklist of companies that need a licence to receive US technology.
stories.why: Commerce is adding Singapore-based Megaspeed to the entity list over alleged Nvidia chip smuggling, Semafor reported on 23 Nov.
stories.source: Nvidia newsroom (via AI Weekly) · 23 Nov; CNBC (via AI Weekly) · 23 Nov

stories.title: Customer-service agent maker Sierra doubles to a $30B valuation
stories.plain: Sierra, the company led by Bret Taylor and Clay Bavor that builds AI agents for customer service, raised $1.75 billion at a $30 billion valuation. That is double its valuation from May.
stories.eng: The Series F was led by Greenoaks and Lightspeed. Sierra says it reached $400M in annualised run-rate revenue in October, with customers including BNY, HSBC, Wells Fargo and JPMorganChase. Its agents handle conversations end to end and take actions in company systems, such as processing returns or account changes.
stories.point: The point: customer service is the first place AI agents are producing large, recurring revenue, and investors are paying for it.
stories.means: Most agent startups are still at the pilot stage, but customer support has clear tasks, measurable outcomes (tickets resolved, cost per contact) and huge existing budgets. $400M of annualised revenue makes Sierra one of the larger pure agent businesses. A $30B valuation is 75 times that revenue, which prices in a lot of future growth during a week when AI stocks are under pressure.
stories.industry: This sits against bubble talk: public AI stocks are in a correction and a senator plans a 'no AI bailouts' resolution, yet private money still flows to agent companies with real revenue. Big banks as customers also show regulated industries are deploying agents for customer-facing work.
stories.you: Support and back-office workflows are where agent jobs and budgets are concentrated. Skills in integrating agents with ticketing, CRM and payment systems, plus guardrails and evaluation, are in demand.
terms: Run-rate revenue
Current monthly revenue multiplied by 12, an estimate of yearly revenue.
Series F
A late-stage funding round, after a company has raised several earlier rounds.
stories.why: Supertake also raised a $20M seed for agents that turn market predictions into stock portfolios via Robinhood and Coinbase.

stories.title: Virginia and Oregon sue SpaceX over Grok's sexual deepfakes
stories.plain: The attorneys general of Virginia and Oregon sued SpaceX, which now owns xAI and X, and its owner Elon Musk, over Grok creating sexualised fake images of real people, including children. They argue the companies told users they were protected when they were not.
stories.eng: Both suits use state consumer-protection law rather than AI-specific statutes: Oregon's Unlawful Trade Practices Act (failing to disclose known defects, unconscionable tactics) and Virginia's Consumer Protection Act (misrepresenting the quality of a service). The complaints say Grok stripped out industry-standard safeguards, marketed a 'spicy mode' and used X as an instant distribution platform. They cite a CCDH study estimating about 3 million sexualised images between 29 Dec 2025 and 8 Jan 2026.
specs: Virginia AG Jay Jones, Oregon AG Dan Rayfield
stories.point: The point: states are using ordinary consumer-protection law to hold AI companies liable for what their models generate.
stories.means: There is no federal AI law, and Congress is still debating whether to override state rules. Consumer-protection acts, however, already ban misleading people about a product's safety, so states can act now without new legislation. The claim is not that a model made a bad image once, but that the company knew about the risk, removed safeguards and kept marketing the product. SpaceX had not responded publicly at the time of reporting.
stories.industry: This adds to a separate class action by abuse victims against xAI and comes as governors push to keep state powers in any federal AI framework. If these theories succeed, safety claims in AI marketing become a legal liability for every lab.
stories.you: If you ship generative features, your safety claims are now evidence. Keep what you say publicly about safeguards matched to what is actually enforced, and log abuse reports and how fast you act on them.
terms: Attorney general
A state's top legal officer, who can sue companies on behalf of the public.
Injunction
A court order requiring a party to do or stop doing something.
stories.why: Musk's xAI is separately suing Minnesota over a law targeting nudification technology.
stories.source: CyberScoop · 23 Nov; CNBC (via AI Weekly) · 23 Nov

stories.title: ML on uterine biopsies flags infertility risk and 5 existing drugs
stories.plain: Researchers used machine learning on uterine tissue samples to sort patients by their chances of pregnancy. The model also pointed to five already-approved drugs that might help those with a poor outlook.
stories.eng: The study analysed 192 endometrial biopsies and separated patients into poor- and good-prognosis groups, which went on to have very different pregnancy rates. Molecular signatures of the poor-prognosis group were then matched against existing medicines to find drugs that might reverse them, a technique known as drug repurposing.
stories.point: The point: ML can turn tissue data into both a prognosis and a shortlist of existing drugs to test, which is much faster than discovering new ones.
stories.means: Endometrial problems are a known cause of failed IVF, but doctors have few tools to predict which patients will struggle. Splitting patients into groups with a 26% versus 66% chance of pregnancy suggests the model is picking up real biology. Repurposing approved drugs matters because their safety is already known, so trials can start sooner. This is one study of 192 samples reported by a secondary outlet; the drug candidates are hypotheses that still need clinical trials.
stories.industry: Drug repurposing with ML is one of the most practical uses of AI in medicine because it skips years of safety testing. Benchmarks like OpenAI's new MedChemBench show labs also want to prove models can reason about chemistry for drug work.
stories.you: Small clinical datasets like this are common in medicine, so careful validation (held-out patients, external cohorts) matters more than model size. If you work on health data, that is where the real engineering effort goes.
terms: Drug repurposing
Finding new uses for medicines already approved for other conditions.
Prognosis
A prediction of how a condition is likely to turn out.
stories.why: OpenAI also released MedChemBench, a 99-problem benchmark for medicinal chemistry, this week.

eras.name: Large language models
eras.short: Models trained to predict the next word turn out to write, translate and code.
eras.how: A transformer is trained on a large share of the public internet to predict the next token. Capabilities appear with scale: GPT-3 could do tasks it was never trained for, given a few examples in the prompt.
eras.built: Autocomplete, text generation APIs, early GitHub Copilot.
eras.broke: Raw models ramble, make things up and do not follow instructions reliably.

eras.name: Chatbots
eras.short: Instruction tuning and human feedback make models useful in a conversation.
eras.how: Fine-tune the base model on examples of good answers, then use reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) so it prefers helpful, safe replies.
eras.built: Chat interfaces, customer support bots, writing assistants.
eras.broke: The model only knows its training data and cannot look anything up or do anything.

eras.name: RAG and tool use
eras.short: Models get access to your documents and to APIs.
eras.how: Retrieval-augmented generation fetches relevant documents and pastes them into the prompt. Function calling lets the model output a structured call to an API you define.
eras.broke: One question, one answer. Multi-step tasks still needed a human driving every step.

eras.name: Workflows
eras.short: Engineers chain model calls into fixed pipelines.
eras.how: You write the steps in code: classify, then retrieve, then draft, then check. The model fills in each step, but the control flow is yours.
eras.built: Document processing pipelines, LangChain-style chains, eval harnesses.
eras.broke: Fixed pipelines break on anything you did not anticipate. Real tasks need the system to decide what to do next.

eras.name: Agents
eras.short: The model decides the next step itself, in a loop with tools.
eras.how: A loop: the model looks at the goal and results so far, picks a tool, runs it, reads the output, repeats until done. Reasoning models that think before answering made these loops far more reliable.
eras.built: Coding agents, computer-use agents, MCP servers that expose tools to any agent.
eras.broke: Agents worked for minutes, then drifted, looped or lost track on long tasks.

eras.name: Autonomous agents
eras.short: Agents run for hours on real work in sandboxes, with little supervision.
eras.how: Better long-horizon training, sandboxed environments, checkpoints and the ability to run tests let an agent own a whole task: open the repo, make the change, run CI, open a pull request.
eras.built: Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity; agents opening PRs while you sleep.
eras.broke: One agent is one thread of work. Large problems need many in parallel.

eras.name: Multi-agent orchestration
eras.short: A planner agent splits work across specialist agents.
eras.how: An orchestrator breaks a goal into subtasks, hands them to worker agents with different tools or prompts, and merges the results.
eras.built: Agent teams for research, code migration and analysis; orchestration frameworks.
eras.broke: Coordination overhead grows fast, and someone still has to check every worker’s output.

eras.name: Agent swarms with verifiers
eras.short: Hundreds to thousands of agents work against an automatic checker that accepts only correct results.
eras.how: Instead of trusting agents, you trust the verifier: a proof checker, test suite or simulator. Agents propose, the verifier filters, survivors get refined. Memory layers start letting agents keep what they learn.
eras.built: 1,000-agent formal proof of Fermat in ~30h; AI-designed quantum circuits beating human designs; Signal's crypto code verified by agents in Lean.
eras.broke: Still open: it only works where a strict automatic check exists.
eras.marks: Fermat formalization (9 Nov 2026), AI quantum circuits (10 Nov 2026), AlphaProof Code on Signal (10 Nov 2026)

eras.name: World models and continual learning
eras.short: Contenders for what comes next: models that learn physics from observation and keep learning after deployment.
eras.how: World models simulate how an environment will change when you act, which lets agents plan in the physical world. Continual learning updates the model from experience without retraining from scratch.
eras.built: Research prototypes, robotics simulation, NeurIPS 2026 workshops.
eras.broke: Not yet reliable outside labs. Watch Frontier for signals.
eras.marks: Genie, V-JEPA, Continual World Models workshop (NeurIPS 2026)
